overview.summary: New Zealand has eight universities and a range of polytechnic and private institutions, smaller cities and a published visa processing time. Work rights during study increased to 25 hours a week.
overview.educationSystem: Qualifications sit on the New Zealand Qualifications and Credentials Framework (NZQCF). Universities offer bachelor’s (level 7), postgraduate diplomas (level 8), master’s (level 9) and doctorates (level 10). Polytechnics and private training establishments offer diplomas and applied degrees.

financialEvidence.requirement: You must show NZD 20,000 for each year of study (or NZD 1,667 per month for courses shorter than a year), plus tuition fees, unless your living costs are already paid or you have an acceptable sponsor.

insurance.requirement: Full medical and travel insurance acceptable to your education provider for your whole stay.

conditions: Up to 25 hours a week during study and full-time in scheduled holidays, depending on the conditions printed on your visa.
Required practical work experience that is part of your course is in addition to these hours.
Job availability varies by city and season. Wages and hours are not guaranteed, so do not depend on work income for tuition.

postStudyRoutes.name: Post-Study Work Visa

duration.value: Up to 3 years, depending on the qualification and study length
duration.label: official

postStudyRoutes.conditions: Recently completed an approved New Zealand qualification. Graduates of degree-level 7 or higher qualifications can work for any employer; non-degree level 7 or lower graduates must work in a related job and the qualification must be on the eligible list. You need at least NZD 5,000 for living costs. Fee NZD 1,670.

postStudyRoutes.name: Accredited Employer Work Visa
postStudyRoutes.conditions: Requires a job offer from an accredited employer that meets wage and other requirements.

postStudyRoutes.name: Residence
postStudyRoutes.conditions: Separate residence pathways have strict criteria. Study does not lead to residence automatically.

lifestyle.text: University halls (often catered) for first-year students, then shared flats. Rental demand is high around the start of each year.
City buses and trains in Auckland and Wellington; many students walk or cycle in smaller cities.
Temperate and changeable; the south is noticeably colder in winter.
Most international students are not eligible for publicly funded healthcare, so insurance is essential.
Generally safe. Learn about earthquake preparedness and outdoor safety.
